prompt.context: Lawn Co. specializes in residential lawn fertilization, weed control, and disease prevention. It is a large US residential lawn care company with approximately 20% market share. Lawn Co. is highly profitable with margins driven through an aggressive focus on cost. However, Lawn Co. has seen little top-line revenue growth in recent years.
prompt.question: Should Lawn Co. focus on organic growth or should it pursue inorganic acquisitions to grow?

clarifying_info.a: Lawn Co. leads with ~20% share; the rest of the market is highly fragmented among many smaller players (see market share exhibit).

clarifying_info.q: What does organic growth mean here?
clarifying_info.a: Organic growth means acquiring new customers through Lawn Co.'s own marketing and sales efforts, not through buying other companies.

clarifying_info.q: What does inorganic growth mean here?
clarifying_info.a: Inorganic growth means acquiring other lawn care companies and inheriting their customer bases.

clarifying_info.q: Is the cost to serve organic vs. inorganic customers the same?
clarifying_info.a: You can assume the cost to serve both types of customers is the same.

exhibits.title: Lawn & Landscaping Market Size
exhibits.shows: A bar/line chart of total US lawn and landscaping market size (residential and commercial) from 1989 to 2007, with CAGR annotations for two periods.

exhibits.title: Lawn Co. Total Revenue (US & Canada)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of Lawn Co. total revenue from 2004 to 2007, with a CAGR annotation.

exhibits.title: Lawn Co. Market Share (2008)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing percent of market revenue among Lawn Co., Fertilizer Co., Weed Co., Care Co., and all others. Total market shown as $4.9B.

exhibits.title: New Customer Counts and Acquisition Costs (2007)
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts side by side: (1) number of new customers acquired organically vs. inorganically in 2007; (2) total cost to acquire those customers organically vs. inorganically in 2007.

exhibits.title: Average Customer Annual Spend (2004–2007)
exhibits.shows: A line chart showing average annual spend per customer from 2004 to 2007, with separate lines for organic and inorganic customers.

exhibits.title: Average Customer Lifetime
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing average customer lifetime in years for organic vs. inorganic customers.

framework: Understand the strategic question: organic vs. inorganic growth — which yields better returns?
Build a profit tree / customer lifetime value (CLV) framework: Net value per customer = Revenue over lifetime − Cost to acquire
Step 1 — Cost to acquire: Calculate cost per new customer for each channel (total acquisition spend ÷ number of new customers)
Step 2 — Revenue per customer: Calculate total spend over lifetime (annual spend × customer lifetime)
Step 3 — Net contribution: Revenue over lifetime − cost to acquire → compare organic vs. inorganic
Consider qualitative factors: market fragmentation (feasibility of acquisitions), customer attrition during acquisition, purchase premiums, scalability of each channel

questions.prompt: How much does it cost to acquire one new customer organically vs. inorganically?
questions.guidance: Interviewee should divide total acquisition cost by number of new customers in each channel. They should round numbers for mental math. The key insight is that inorganic customers cost significantly more per head to acquire.

math.setup: Cost per customer = Total acquisition cost ÷ Number of new customers acquired

questions.prompt: How much does each type of customer spend over the course of their tenure with Lawn Co.?
questions.guidance: Interviewee should multiply average annual spend by average customer lifetime. They should round to easy numbers. Strong candidates may ask whether cost to serve is the same for both types.

math.setup: Total lifetime spend = Average annual spend × Average customer lifetime (years)
math.answer: Organic: ~$800 lifetime spend; Inorganic: ~$760 lifetime spend

questions.prompt: Given the acquisition costs and lifetime revenue, which type of customer is more attractive for Lawn Co.?
questions.guidance: Interviewee should calculate net contribution per customer (lifetime revenue minus acquisition cost). Organic customers yield a higher net contribution. Strong candidates will note that this assumes equal cost to serve; they may also discuss qualitative considerations such as purchase premiums and customer attrition during acquisitions.

math.setup: Net contribution = Lifetime revenue − Cost to acquire
math.answer: Organic customers yield ~$700 net contribution vs. ~$400 for inorganic — organic growth is more attractive on a per-customer basis

brainstorming.prompt: Why might inorganic (acquired) customers cost more to acquire per head?

categories.name: Purchase premium
ideas: Acquiring companies requires paying a control premium above intrinsic value
Sellers price in future cash flows, reducing acquirer's upside

categories.name: Customer attrition
ideas: Some customers leave during ownership transition ('don't want to be a Lawn Co. customer')
Brand or service-level differences cause churn post-acquisition

categories.name: Integration costs
ideas: Systems integration, rebranding, and staff alignment add hidden costs
Overlap in service territories reduces efficiency gains

recommendation: Lawn Co. should prioritize organic growth over inorganic acquisitions
Organic customers cost ~$100 to acquire vs. ~$360 inorganically, and generate comparable or higher lifetime spend, yielding ~$700 net contribution per customer vs. ~$400 for acquired customers
At the same time, Lawn Co. is growing at ~4% p.a. while the market grows at ~5%, suggesting room to increase organic marketing investment to capture share
risks: Organic growth may be slower to scale if marketing channels are already saturated
Inorganic acquisitions could be justified if synergies (cost to serve reductions, geographic expansion) substantially improve the economics
Fragmentation of remaining market may limit high-quality acquisition targets anyway
next_steps: Investigate why Lawn Co.'s organic growth (3.9% CAGR) is lagging market growth (5.1%) — identify which customer segments or geographies are underperforming
Assess whether increasing organic marketing spend can close the growth gap cost-effectively
Model acquisition scenarios with synergy assumptions to determine if any targets change the inorganic economics
